query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A simple, single intervention of applying a fluorine‐containing surface treatment (e.g., via spraying a dilute NaF aqueous solution) to the cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy will promote the formation of a thin, dense, and adherent protective oxide film during subsequent high-temperature exposure, thereby markedly improving its oxidation resistance without compromising its useful mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy that in its untreated state exhibits 8–16% RT tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C but suffers from poor oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Surface treatment by applying a fluorine-containing solution (e.g., spray deposition of a NaF-containing aqueous solution), followed by a controlled isothermal oxidation step.
generation.conditions: Oxidation performed at 1000 °C in air (or oxygen-containing atmosphere) for a duration on the order of 100 hours; mechanical properties evaluated under strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1 at high temperature and standard tensile conditions at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: A thin, dense, and continuous oxide scale formed on the surface (mediated by the fluorine-induced reactions) that prevents rapid oxygen ingress.
generation.mechanism: The fluorine treatment chemically alters the surface such that during high-temperature exposure, it promotes the formation of a protective oxide layer (for instance, by forming intermediate fluorides that convert to tightly adherent, stable oxides of Ti, Hf, or Ta). This barrier limits oxygen diffusivity into the bulk without affecting the underlying microstructure that governs mechanical behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated cast alloys, the fluorine-treated specimens will show a substantially lower weight gain (indicative of reduced oxidation rates) and maintain similar room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength, effectively extending the alloy’s applicability at elevated temperatures.
generation.baseline: Untreated cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy, known for its useful mechanical performance but poor oxygen resistance at elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: Intervention effectiveness is expected when applied only as a surface treatment (without altering bulk composition) and tested at around 1000 °C in oxidizing environments over timescales (e.g., ~100 hours) relevant to high-temperature applications; mechanical loading should remain within the established strain-rate windows (10^−4–10^−2 s^−1).
generation.uncertainty: It is uncertain whether the exact nature of the protective oxide film (its chemical composition and long-term adherence) in the HfNbTaTiZr system will mimic that observed in fluorine‐treated TiAl alloys; the optimum treatment parameters (fluorine concentration, application method, and oxidation schedule) may require adjustment to preserve bulk mechanical performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy samples: one set receives the fluorine-containing surface spray treatment while the control set is left untreated. Expose both sets to an isothermal oxidation treatment at 1000 °C for 100 hours in air. After exposure, measure the oxidation weight gain, analyze surface and cross-sectional microstructures (using SEM/EDS/XRD) to identify the presence and integrity of any protective oxide layers, and perform tensile tests (room temperature and high-temperature) to assess whether mechanical properties are maintained.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and phase composition
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the fluorine-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxidation (e.g., weight gain comparable to untreated samples) or if the protective oxide film is nonuniform/delaminated, or if mechanical performance (ductility or yield strength) is degraded relative to controls, then the hypothesis will be refuted.

cited_evidence.text: In-depth analyses of the anti-oxidation behavior and structure of γ-TiAl alloys are of great significant for their maintenance and repair in engineering applications. In this work, fluorine-treated Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys and fluorine-treated oxidized specimens with artificial defects were prepared by isothermal oxidation treatment at 1000 °C. Several characterization methods, including SEM, EDS, XRD and TEM, were used to evaluate the surface microstructure of the fluorine-treated Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys and fluorine-treated oxidized specimens with artificial defects. The results indicate that the fluorine promoted the formation of an outer protective film of Al2O3, which significantly improved the oxidation resistance. The microcracks of oxidized specimens with the artificial defects provided a rapid diffusion passage for Ti and O elements during the 1000 °C/2 h isothermal oxidation treatment process, resulting in the quick growth of TiO2 toward the outside. The fine Al2O3 constituted a continuous film after the 1000 °C/100 h isothermal oxidation treatment. In this study, we executed a simple and effective strategy involving a two-step spraying and oxidation process to produce Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys with a dense Al2O3 film for application at high temperatures. The main results are as follows: (1)The oxidation resistance was significantly improved due to the formation of a protective Al2O3 film induced by the fluorine effect during isothermal oxidation at 1000 °C (6.03 mg/cm2 weight gain for the bare Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys, but 0.81 mg/cm2 for the fluorine-treated Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys).(2)The Ti diffused along the artificial microcracks, resulting in a quick growth of TiO2 in a short time (2 h), while a continuous Al2O3 film was generated underneath the oxide scale during further isothermal oxidation (100 h).(3)The Al2O3 particles between the alloy and continuous Al2O3 film were reflected in the γ-TiAl and α2-Ti3Al phases, which improved the adhesion of the oxide scale (fluorine-treated specimen had a deep yellow oxide scale on the surface without any exfoliation). These findings represent significant progress towards reducing the high temperature oxidation resistance of TiAl intermetallics by surface fluorine modification.

notes.research_context: The research group asking this question works on high-entropy (multi-principal-element) alloys for high-temperature applications.
